candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9533 malware probability, but the supplied evidence does not support a high-confidence cryptojacking call on its own. All 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, with individual SHAP contributions between +0.006070 and +0.015024. Their sum is a diffuse, additive push. No single feature dominates. Seventeen of the twenty n-grams have a relative frequency of 0.000000, so they are effectively absent from the binary. Their positive SHAP values likely mean the model treats the absence of these patterns as typical of the malware class, not that the binary contains mining-specific code. Only POP SUB (+0.014270), POP PUSH (+0.012869) and DEC PUSH (+0.006841) were observed, each at a frequency of 0.005051. These are generic stack and register manipulation sequences found in function prologues, epilogues and ordinary compiled code. They are not characteristic of cryptographic hashing or mining loops. The evidence also lists no function locations, no API names, and no strings. It contains no rotate, shift-heavy or wide-arithmetic sequences typical of hashing kernels. XOR SHL (+0.006070) and the XOR-related n-grams (XOR CALL, XOR XOR, XOR MOV, XOR CMOVNZ) have zero observed frequency, so they cannot be treated as evidence of hash-like computation. The high model probability suggests the binary is anomalous or resembles the malware training distribution, but the evidence cannot show that the sample is a cryptojacker specifically. The result is inconclusive and needs corroboration.
